description: Prophethood from Adam to Muhammad, the revealed holy books, and the four named angels.
content_html:
Risalah: Allah’s Communication with Humanity

Risalah is one of the most important concepts in Islamic theology. It means prophethood or “message,” and it refers to the way Allah has chosen to guide human beings throughout history: not by making His will obvious to everyone directly, but by selecting certain individuals to receive and convey His revelation. Without Risalah, humans would have no reliable knowledge of how Allah wants them to live. The Qur’an states in Surah al-Imran (3:144): “Muhammad is not but a messenger; there have been messengers before him.” This verse places Muhammad within a long line of prophets and insists that prophethood itself did not begin or end with any single individual — though it did find its culmination in him.

The Prophets: From Adam to Muhammad

Islamic tradition teaches that Allah sent prophets to every community throughout history, beginning with Adam. Muslims use two Arabic terms: a nabi is a prophet who receives revelation for his own community; a rasul is a messenger who brings a new scripture or law. Some prophets are named in the Qur’an; Muslims believe there may have been many thousands more. The following are key figures:

  • Adam — the first human and the first prophet. Allah created him and appointed him as His khalifa (steward or representative) on earth. Adam represents the original covenant between humanity and Allah.
  • Ibrahim (Abraham) — described as a hanif (one who turns purely to Allah, rejecting polytheism). He is considered the father of the prophets and rebuilt the Kaaba in Mecca with his son Isma’il as a house of pure monotheistic worship.
  • Isma’il — Ibrahim’s son and co-builder of the Kaaba in Mecca. He is also revered as the ancestor of the Arab people and, through them, of the Prophet Muhammad.
  • Musa (Moses) — the prophet to whom Allah revealed the Torah (Tawrat) and the Ten Commandments. He led the Israelites out of slavery and taught them the law of God.
  • Dawud (David) — given the Psalms (Zabur) by Allah and remembered for his victory over Goliath and his role as a just king.
  • Isa (Jesus) — a highly revered prophet and messenger in Islam, born miraculously of the Virgin Mary. Muslims believe Isa was given the Injil (Gospel) and performed miracles by Allah’s permission. Crucially, Islam does not teach that Isa is divine or the Son of God — he is a prophet, not a deity.
Key Fact

Adam is described as Allah’s khalifa (steward on earth). Ibrahim is described as a hanif (one who turns purely to Allah). Both terms are specific Qur’anic descriptions with exam significance: they indicate the role or spiritual status of these prophets rather than simply their identity.

Muhammad: The Seal of the Prophets

Muhammad (peace be upon him) holds a unique position in Islamic belief. He is known as the seal of the prophets (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). This means that prophetic revelation ended with Muhammad; no new prophet will bring a new message from Allah after him. The Qur’an was revealed to him over 23 years beginning in a cave on Mount Hira, as described in Surah al-Alaq (Surah 96), the first revelation.

Islam teaches that the original message given to all previous prophets was essentially the same: submit to the one God. Over time, earlier revelations became distorted or incomplete. The Qur’an, revealed to Muhammad, is understood as the final, fully preserved and undistorted message from Allah. Surah al-Ma’idah (5:46) confirms the continuity of revelation: “We sent after them Isa the son of Maryam, confirming that which came before him in the Torah.”

Shi’a Muslims believe that after the Prophet Muhammad — who was the last prophet — authority over the Muslim community passed to a line of twelve Imams descended from the Prophet through his son-in-law Ali. These Imams are not prophets (prophethood ended with Muhammad), but they are considered infallible guides whose interpretation of the Qur’an and Islamic law is authoritative.

This belief distinguishes Shi’a Islam sharply from Sunni Islam, which does not accept the concept of infallible Imams. For Sunni Muslims, guidance after the Prophet comes from the Qur’an, the Sunnah (the Prophet’s example), and the scholarly community (Ulema). Both traditions, however, agree that prophethood itself is definitively closed with Muhammad.

The Holy Books: Kutub

Islam teaches that Allah revealed scriptures (Kutub) to various prophets throughout history. Four are given special prominence:

  • Sahifah — the scrolls revealed to Ibrahim (and according to some traditions, Adam). These are the earliest recorded revelation.
  • Tawrat — the Torah, revealed to Musa. The original Tawrat was the word of Allah; Muslims believe the version now in the Torah has been subject to alteration over time.
  • Zabur — the Psalms, revealed to Dawud. Surah al-Ma’idah (5:46) confirms the continuity of these earlier books with the final message.
  • Injil — the Gospel, revealed to Isa. Muslims believe the original Injil was a pure message from Allah; they do not regard the four Gospels of the Christian New Testament as identical to the original Injil.

The Qur’an is the last and final revealed scripture. Unlike previous scriptures, which Muslims believe became distorted over time, the Qur’an is held to be perfectly preserved in its original form. Surah al-Alaq (Surah 96) records the first revelation: “Read! In the name of your Lord who created.”

The Angels: Allah’s Messengers in Creation

Islam teaches that Allah created angels (mala’ikah) from light before He created humanity. Angels are immortal, free from sin, and without free will — they carry out Allah’s commands perfectly and without deviation. Surah Fatir (35:1) describes the angels as “messengers with wings.” The belief in angels is one of the six Sunni articles of faith. Surah an-Nahl (16:102) specifically identifies Jibril as the one who conveyed the Qur’an to the Prophet.

Four angels have named roles that are essential exam knowledge:

  • Jibril — the chief angel and the angel of revelation. He delivered the Qur’an word by word to Muhammad over 23 years.
  • Izra’il — the angel of death, responsible for taking the final breath of every soul at the moment of death.
  • Mika’il — the bringer of rain and sustenance. He is associated with provision and the physical wellbeing of creation. (The guardian of paradise in Islamic tradition is Ridwan, not Mika’il.)
  • Israfil — the angel who will blow the trumpet on the Day of Judgement to signal the resurrection of all souls.

Alongside the four named angels, Islam teaches that every human being has recording angels (Kiraman Katibin — “honourable scribes”) on their left and right shoulders. The angel on the right records good deeds; the one on the left records sins. These records will be read out on the Day of Judgement.

For many Muslims, the awareness of recording angels acts as a powerful moral guide. Knowing that no action — however private — goes unrecorded encourages honesty, compassion and avoidance of wrongdoing even when no human witness is present. This belief connects the Islamic doctrine of angels directly to ethics and everyday conduct.

Key Fact

The four named angels are: Jibril (revelation), Izra’il (death), Mika’il (rain and sustenance), Israfil (trumpet on the Day of Judgement). Surah Fatir (35:1) describes angels as messengers with wings; Surah an-Nahl (16:102) links Jibril to the revelation of the Qur’an.
exam_tip_html: Examiners expect you to be precise about the roles of the four named angels — a very common error is to confuse Mika’il (rain and sustenance) with Izra’il (death) or Israfil (the trumpet). When Describing or Outlining prophethood, make sure you explain what ‘seal of the prophets’ means: it is not just that Muhammad was great, but that he was the last, meaning no new prophetic revelation will come. For a 15-mark Discuss question about whether all prophets are equally important, you can argue the Muslim position that all prophets bring the same essential message, while also presenting the view that Muhammad has a uniquely final status. Use Surah 3:144 and Surah 96 as source anchors. Accurate spelling matters for SPaG: ‘Risalah’, ‘Jibril’, ‘Israfil’, ‘khalifa’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Risalah (prophethood) is Allah’s way of guiding humanity through chosen messengers. Key prophets include Adam (khalifa), Ibrahim (hanif), Musa, Dawud, Isa and Muhammad, the ‘seal of the prophets’ whose message is final and preserved in the Qur’an.
  • The Kutub (holy books) — Sahifah, Tawrat, Zabur, Injil and the Qur’an — all convey the same essential message from Allah; only the Qur’an is believed to be perfectly preserved in its original form.
  • The four named angels are Jibril (revelation), Izra’il (death), Mika’il (rain and sustenance) and Israfil (the trumpet on Judgement Day); belief in angels is one of the six Sunni articles of faith.

practice_questions.text: State the Arabic term for the concept of prophethood in Islam.
Describe the role of the angel Jibril in Islamic belief.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: Jibril is the chief angel in Islam (1 mark) who was responsible for conveying Allah's revelation to the prophets, including delivering the Qur'an word by word to Muhammad (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline Muslim beliefs about the role and importance of the holy books (Kutub).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks: Allah revealed scriptures to various prophets throughout history (1 mark); these include the Tawrat (Moses), Zabur (David), Injil (Jesus) and the Qur'an (Muhammad) (1 mark); Muslims believe previous scriptures became distorted over time, while the Qur'an is the final, perfectly preserved message from Allah (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muhammad is considered to hold a special position among the prophets in Islamic belief.
practice_questions.marks: Possible points: Muhammad is described as the 'seal of the prophets' (Khatam an-Nabiyyin) — meaning he is the last and final prophet, closing the line of prophethood (1+1 mark). The Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad as the final, undistorted and perfectly preserved scripture, making his message authoritative for all time (1+1 mark). Surah al-Imran (3:144) places Muhammad within the line of prophets while also indicating his unique role as the culmination of prophethood (1+1 mark). Surah al-Alaq (Surah 96) records the first revelation to Muhammad, marking the beginning of a new era of divine guidance (1+1 mark). [6 marks: 3 marks per reason — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'All prophets in Islam are equally important.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: All prophets receive their message from the same Allah and convey the same essential monotheistic message; the Qur'an says messengers were sent to every community; each prophet served a vital role in his time and context; Islam forbids making distinctions that dishonour any prophet. Arguments against: The Qur'an (3:144) identifies Muhammad as the final messenger, giving him unique finality; Ibrahim is called the 'father of the prophets' and a hanif; Isa is described as performing miracles by divine permission; the Qur'an itself mentions that some prophets were given preference over others; the revealed book of each messenger had different scope and duration. Mastering: Both sides developed with named prophets, specific roles (khalifa, hanif, seal), sources (Surah 3:144, Surah 96, Surah 5:46), explicit weighing, and justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with sourcing; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or limited. Emerging: Brief, unsupported. [15 marks: SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: State the role of the angel Israfil on the Day of Judgement.
practice_questions.marks: Israfil will blow the trumpet to signal the resurrection of all souls on the Day of Judgement. [1 mark]

knowledge_checks.q: Which title is given to Muhammad to indicate that he is the last prophet?
Which angel is responsible for taking the final breath of every soul at death?
Adam was appointed by Allah as His _____ (steward or representative) on earth.
The Qur'an was first revealed to Muhammad in Surah _____, beginning with the word 'Read!'
Match each prophet to the holy book revealed to them:

flashcard_questions.q: What does Risalah mean in Islamic belief?
flashcard_questions.a: Prophethood — Allah's way of communicating guidance to humanity through chosen messengers.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'seal of the prophets' mean as a title for Muhammad?
flashcard_questions.a: That Muhammad is the last and final prophet — no new prophet will come after him.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'khalifa' mean, and which prophet holds this title?
flashcard_questions.a: Steward or representative of Allah on earth; the title is given to Adam.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'hanif' mean, and which prophet is described this way?
flashcard_questions.a: One who turns purely to Allah, rejecting polytheism; Ibrahim is described as a hanif.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Kaaba, and which prophets rebuilt it?
flashcard_questions.a: The house of Allah in Mecca; it was rebuilt by Ibrahim and his son Isma'il.

flashcard_questions.q: Which prophet is described as 'not divine but a messenger' in Islamic belief?
flashcard_questions.a: Isa (Jesus) — revered as a prophet and given the Injil, but not divine.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four holy books in Islam and the prophet each was revealed to.
What does the Qur'an teach that distinguishes it from earlier scriptures?
flashcard_questions.a: It is the final, perfectly preserved message from Allah — earlier scriptures became distorted.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of Jibril in Islamic belief?
flashcard_questions.a: Chief angel and angel of revelation; conveyed the Qur'an to Muhammad.

flashcard_questions.q: What will Israfil do on the Day of Judgement?
flashcard_questions.a: Blow the trumpet to signal the resurrection of all souls.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the recording angels in Islam?
flashcard_questions.a: They record every human deed — good and bad — to be read on the Day of Judgement.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do Shi'a Muslims believe in the twelve Imams after the Prophet?
flashcard_questions.a: They believe authority passed to divinely appointed, infallible Imams from the Prophet's family.

glossary_terms.definition: The Islamic concept of prophethood — Allah's way of communicating guidance to humanity through chosen messengers.
The first human being and first prophet in Islam, created by Allah and appointed as His khalifa (steward) on earth.
The cube-shaped structure in the Grand Mosque in Mecca, believed by Muslims to be the house of Allah first built by Ibrahim and Isma'il.
The title given to the Prophet Muhammad in the Qur'an, meaning he is the last and final prophet — no prophet will come after him.
In Shi'a Islam, the twelve divinely appointed leaders descended from the Prophet's family, believed to be infallible interpreters of Islamic law and scripture.
The Arabic term for the holy books, the revealed scriptures sent by Allah to His prophets throughout history.
The holy book of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the final, perfectly preserved word of Allah revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Jibril.
The chief angel in Islam, responsible for conveying Allah's revelation to the prophets. Also known as Gabriel in Christian tradition.
